notes.meaning: When Queen Mother Athaliah learned that her son Ahaziah had died, she moved quickly to kill off all his sons and heirs so she could seize the throne for herself. Because her northern royal family had just been wiped out by Jehu, she lashed out to destroy the house of David in Judah as well. God had promised that David would always have an heir on the throne, so her murderous grab for power threatened that holy promise.

Princess Jehosheba, Ahaziah's half-sister and wife to the high priest, secretly snatched the infant prince Joash from the nursery before the murderers reached him. She hid the baby boy and his nurse in a palace storeroom where bedding was kept. Her brave action spared the one remaining heir of David's line from Athaliah's bloody purge.

Joash remained safely tucked away in the living rooms of the temple priests for six whole years. During that time, Athaliah ruled Judah as an unlawful tyrant, likely assuming all the royal heirs were dead. Even when God's plans seem hidden or hanging by a thread, he quietly preserves his people.

In the seventh year of Athaliah's rule, the high priest Jehoiada began a careful plan to restore the rightful king. He gathered the commanders of the foreign mercenaries and royal palace guards into the temple courts under strict secrecy. Before revealing young Joash to them, he bound these military leaders under a sacred oath of loyalty.

Jehoiada took advantage of the Sabbath shift change, when one group of guards arrived while another was scheduled to leave. He assigned one third of the incoming shift to guard the palace and other gateways, preventing Athaliah's palace troops from interfering. The two units who would normally go home were held back in the temple courts to surround and protect the young king.

The priest commanded the armed guards to stay right beside the young boy wherever he moved. Anyone from outside who tried to push through their protective lines was to be killed immediately. This airtight ring of security ensured the boy would not be assassinated before he could be crowned.

The army captains carried out Jehoiada's orders down to the smallest detail. They assembled all their men—both those arriving for duty on the Sabbath and those scheduled to go off duty—and brought them to the high priest in the temple.

To keep their secret safe, the guards had entered the temple grounds without their weapons. Jehoiada then handed out the spears and shields that King David had captured long ago and stored as offerings in the sanctuary. It was fitting that David's own weapons were used to protect David's young heir.

The armed guards formed an unbroken wall of defense across the inner court, stretching from the north side of the temple to the south side. They took up their stations by the great altar of burnt offering, ready to defend the area where the king would appear. Everything was now ready to bring the rightful prince out into the open.

Jehoiada led the boy out, set the royal crown on his head, and handed him the Testimony—a written copy of God's holy law. The priests poured oil on him to show God had chosen him, and the gathered crowd began to clap and shout, 'Long live the king!' By receiving God's law at his coronation, Joash was reminded that even an earthly king must rule under God's Word.

Athaliah heard the roaring cheer of the crowds and the blast of the trumpets, so she rushed alone into the temple courts to investigate. She was shocked to see the young boy standing on the king's royal platform, surrounded by army officers and joyful citizens. In fury and terror, she tore her clothes and cried out that a rebellion was taking place.

Jehoiada ordered the army captains to escort Athaliah outside the temple walls between two lines of armed soldiers. He warned them to execute anyone who tried to defend her, but insisted she must not be killed inside the sacred grounds. God's sanctuary was holy and was not to be defiled with human blood.

The soldiers opened a path and led Athaliah out toward the royal stables near the palace gates. There, away from the holy temple, she was executed for her crimes and usurpation. Her violent end near the horse gate echoed the death of her wicked mother, Queen Jezebel.

Jehoiada then led the nation into two solemn agreements, or covenants. First, the king and the people renewed their commitment to the Lord, promising to serve him faithfully and abandon false gods. Second, the king and the people made a civil covenant with each other, where the king pledged to rule justly and the people pledged to obey him.

Immediately following the covenant, the people tore down the local temple built for the pagan god Baal. They smashed its altars and carved images to dust, and killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, right in front of his ruined altars. Jehoiada then stationed guards at the Lord's temple to protect God's house from any retaliatory attacks.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the text never explicitly credits Athaliah with building this Baal temple or practicing Baal worship, suggesting the coup may have had political as well as religious motivations.

notes.meaning: With the city secure, Jehoiada and the army officers escorted the seven-year-old king down from Mount Moriah into the royal palace. They entered through the Gate of the Guards, and Joash was placed upon the royal throne of David. This public act formally completed his crowning as the ruler of Judah.

The entire nation celebrated with great joy, and peace returned to the streets of Jerusalem. The dark reign of Athaliah had ended, and she had received justice for her murders. God had once again preserved the royal line of David, just as he had promised.

Joash was only seven years old when his reign began. Because he was so young, he depended entirely on the godly guidance of the high priest Jehoiada. A leader's success often depends on having faithful, God-fearing advisers.
